newsitem.title: USA: New York Senate proposes savings plan for college.
newsitem.headline: New York Senate proposes savings plan for college.

text.p: The New York State Senate on Monday proposed a savings plan that aimed to make both public and private colleges more affordable for the middle-class that stood in contrast with the governor's plan to hike tuition.

Republican Gov George Pataki has suggested raising tuition at the state's public universities by $400 a year and cutting state aid for New York's neediest students as part of his fiscal 1998 budget. Both proposals that have been sharply criticized.

Senate Majority Leader Joseph Bruno (R-Troy) said the savings plan would have two accounts, one of which would make contributions and interest earnings exempt from state taxes. Federal taxes on interest would be deferred until the money was withdrawn.

A second program would enable families to lock-in current tuition rates at the State University of New York, the City University of New York and community colleges by making lump sum or installment payments. They would qualify for the same state and federal tax benefits.

Noting that state Comptroller H. Carl McCall, a Democrat, Assemblyman Paul Tonoko, D-Amsterdam, and the Senate Minority Leader also had proposed college savings plans, Bruno said: "It's clear there is agreement that we should create a tuition savings plan to help make a college education more affordable for middle-class families in New York."
The Senate's plan calls for a nine-member oversight board that would select a private institution to manage and invest the funds in the accounts.

The panel would be chaired by the governor's appointee. It would also include the commissioner of education, the president of the Higher Education Services Corp, the chairman of the Dormitory Authority, the state comptroller, the superintendent of banks, the superintendent of insurance, and three members of the private sector selected by the governor and legislative leaders.
